results.result: IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies are less pathogenic than IgG1 autoantibodies in TTP models. Both IgG4 and IgG1 variants with similar binding kinetics to ADAMTS13 induced significant reduction in ADAMTS13 activity, but IgG4-treated mice recovered significantly faster than IgG1-treated mice in both WT and FcγR-humanized mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 provide converging experimental evidence from multiple mouse models (WT and hFCGR-Tg) showing that IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies are less pathogenic than IgG1 variants. The data demonstrate similar initial inhibition but faster recovery with IgG4, supporting the conclusion (C44) that IgG4 subclass switching represents a protective mechanism in TTP.

results.result: Activating FcγR-mediated effector function enhances the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies. FcγRα-null and Fcer1g-/- mice showed faster recovery of ADAMTS13 activity compared to WT mice. N297A variants (reduced FcγR binding) were less pathogenic than GASDALIE variants (enhanced FcγR binding), suggesting that FcγR-mediated depletion of ADAMTS13-autoantibody complexes exacerbates disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 provide consistent experimental evidence from multiple genetic knockout models and engineered antibody variants demonstrating that FcγR engagement enhances anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody pathogenicity. The data support the mechanistic interpretation (C52) that FcγR-mediated effector function depletes ADAMTS13-autoantibody immune complexes, though this mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Analysis of TTP patient samples reveals that IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies confer relatively less ADAMTS13 depletion compared to IgG1 autoantibodies. While most TTP patients have both IgG1 and IgG4 autoantibodies with inverse correlation, only IgG1 autoantibodies show significant inverse correlation with ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels. IgG4-dominant patients have higher ADAMTS13 antigen levels despite similar activity levels compared to IgG1-dominant patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C62 present a comprehensive analysis of 44 TTP patient samples with consistent findings across multiple measurements (ELISA, activity assays, correlation analyses). The data support the conclusion (C63) that IgG4 autoantibodies cause less ADAMTS13 depletion, though the correlational nature of patient data limits causal inference. The findings are consistent with the mouse model results.

results.result: IgG4 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies are not less pathogenic than IgG1 in PF models, and FcγR deficiency increases pathogenicity. PF patients have predominantly IgG4 autoantibodies that share binding epitopes with IgG1 autoantibodies. In mouse models, PF24-9(IgG4) tended to be more pathogenic than IgG1 at reduced doses, and FcγRα-null mice showed more severe lesions and increased neutrophil infiltration, suggesting an FcγR-mediated protective mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C87 provide patient data showing IgG4 dominance and shared epitopes (C67-C72), and experimental data from multiple mouse models demonstrating that FcγR deficiency exacerbates disease (C83-C85). The data support the conclusion (C87) of an FcγR-mediated protective mechanism in PF, contrasting with the TTP findings. However, the claim that IgG4 'tends to be more pathogenic' (C83) is based on limited data at reduced antibody doses.

results.result: Anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies with reduced FcγR binding (N297A) are more pathogenic than those with enhanced FcγR binding (GASDALIE) in multiple mouse models. N297A variants induced more severe ear lesions, inflammation, and neutrophil infiltration compared to GASDALIE variants in hFCGR-Tg mice, and showed slower recovery in nude mice. This protective effect of Fc-FcγR interaction was observed across different mouse strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 provide extensive experimental evidence from multiple mouse models (hFCGR-Tg, nude, FcγRα-null) using two different anti-Dsg1 clones and multiple readouts (histology, ear measurements, flow cytometry). The data consistently demonstrate that enhanced FcγR binding reduces pathogenicity in PF models, supporting the conclusion (C91) that Fc-FcγR interaction attenuates anti-Dsg1 autoantibody pathogenicity.

results.result: FcγR-mediated effector function promotes clearance of immune complexes and dead keratinocytes in PF models. GASDALIE variants were depleted faster than N297A variants in FcγR-sufficient mice, with higher immune complex levels observed with N297A treatment. N297A-treated mice and FcγRα-null mice showed more epidermal blistering and dead keratinocytes, suggesting that FcγR-mediated clearance promotes tissue repair.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C102 provide multiple lines of evidence (serum antibody depletion, immune complex levels, TUNEL staining) supporting the mechanism (C103) that FcγR-mediated effector function promotes clearance of dead keratinocytes. The data are consistent across different mouse models and time points. However, the mechanistic link between immune complex clearance and keratinocyte clearance is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: A non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 antibody variant optimized for FcγR-mediated effector function (PF1-2-22 GASDALIE) can attenuate skin lesions induced by pathogenic anti-Dsg1 antibodies (PF1-8-15 N297A). Co-administration of the non-pathogenic GASDALIE variant reduced skin lesions, epidermal blistering, and apoptotic keratinocytes, suggesting therapeutic potential through enhanced clearance of apoptotic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 provide experimental evidence that non-pathogenic GASDALIE antibodies reduce lesions and apoptotic keratinocytes when co-administered with pathogenic N297A antibodies. The data support the therapeutic concept (C5, C106-C107), though the mechanism is inferred from the combination of this result with prior findings on immune complex clearance. The therapeutic potential requires further validation.

results.result: The IgG4 subclass and Fc-FcγR interaction have opposite impacts on autoantibody pathogenicity in TTP versus PF. In TTP, IgG4 and reduced FcγR binding are protective because FcγR-mediated depletion of ADAMTS13 synergizes with blocking function. In PF, IgG4 and reduced FcγR binding are harmful because FcγR-mediated clearance of immune complexes and dead keratinocytes promotes tissue repair. This demonstrates that the impact of IgG subclass depends on disease context.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 and C147-C152 synthesize the major findings from both disease models, providing a coherent framework for understanding the opposite effects. The mechanistic explanations (C151-C152) are well-supported by the experimental data, though they represent inferences from multiple lines of evidence rather than direct demonstrations. The conclusion (C153) about the importance of examining IgG subclass effects in disease context is well-justified.

results.result: IgG4 has unique structural and functional properties including low affinity to FcγRs, lack of complement activation, and reduced immune complex formation due to Fab-arm exchange. These properties make IgG4 the least potent human IgG subclass for FcγR-mediated antibody effector function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C12 describe established properties of IgG4 supported by citations and binding data (C45). This represents well-established background knowledge that provides context for the study's findings. The binding data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C confirm these properties for the antibodies used in this study.

results.result: IgG4 is the dominant IgG subclass in IgG4-mediated autoimmune diseases including TTP and PF, where autoantibodies target ADAMTS13 and Dsg1 respectively. IgG4 autoantibody levels correlate with disease activity, and both polyclonal and monoclonal autoantibodies are pathogenic in vitro and in animal models.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C27 summarize established knowledge about IgG4-mediated diseases supported by extensive citations. This provides essential background for the study but represents prior work rather than new findings. The claims are well-supported by the literature cited.

results.result: Prior literature presents mixed evidence about whether IgG4 is protective or pathogenic in autoimmune diseases. Some studies suggest IgG4 is protective (myasthenia gravis, allergy), while others show IgG4 is pathogenic (TTP, PF). The relationship between IgG subclass and pathogenicity has been unclear due to confounding factors like epitope differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 and C28-C32 accurately summarize prior literature showing conflicting evidence about IgG4's role, supported by appropriate citations. This establishes the rationale for the current study but does not represent new findings. The summary is accurate and provides important context.

results.result: Anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies are pathogenic in the form of scFv and Fab fragments, and adoptive transfer of intact antibodies is sufficient to induce pemphigus in adult mice. The adult mouse model reproduces clinical, histological, and immunological features of PF including epidermal blistering, leukocyte infiltration, and IgG deposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 describe validation of the adult PF mouse model used in the study. The data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, 3) demonstrate that the model recapitulates key features of human disease. Claim C33 cites prior work showing Fab fragments are pathogenic, which is confirmed in this study (C75). This represents important methodological validation.

results.result: FcγRs play critical roles in antibody function across different contexts. Activating FcγRs mediate effector functions and contribute to autoimmune pathology, while their ablation or overexpression of inhibitory FcγRIIB can be protective. Different antibody types (effector, agonistic, blocking) are differentially impacted by Fc-FcγR interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 summarize established knowledge about FcγR biology supported by citations. This provides essential background for interpreting the study's findings but represents prior work. The summary accurately reflects the literature and establishes the conceptual framework for the study.

results.result: Prior literature indicates that IgG1 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies are found in healthy subjects and endemic PF patients, while accumulation of IgG4 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies is a key step in disease development. Binding epitope is critical for anti-Dsg1 autoantibody pathogenicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 accurately summarize prior literature on PF pathogenesis supported by citations. This provides context for the current study's investigation of IgG subclass effects but represents established knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Both IgG1 and IgG4 anti-Dsg1 antibodies induce epidermal blistering and leukocyte infiltration in hFCGR-Tg mice, and both can reach skin tissues at comparable levels as detected by immunofluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 provide basic characterization showing that both IgG subclasses can induce disease and reach target tissues. This is important for establishing that observed differences are not due to differential tissue accessibility. The data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D, E) support these claims.

results.result: Both 'stable' and 'active' PF patient groups have more IgG4 than IgG1 autoantibodies, with 'active' patients having higher autoantibody levels regardless of subclass.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 provide additional characterization of the PF patient cohort showing that IgG4 dominance is consistent across disease states, though active disease is associated with higher overall autoantibody levels. The data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) support these descriptive findings.

results.result: Prior literature on TTP shows mixed findings: IgG4-dominant samples have stronger ADAMTS13 inhibition, but patients with high IgG1/low IgG4 have higher mortality. IgG1/IgG3 titers correlate with acute disease severity, and subclass switching from IgG1 to IgG4 occurs during remission. These findings are consistent with the current study's results.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 accurately summarize prior literature on IgG subclasses in TTP, supported by appropriate citations. The authors correctly note that these findings are consistent with their results, though the prior literature did not directly compare matched IgG1 and IgG4 antibodies as done in the current study.

results.result: Prior literature shows IgG4 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies correlate with PF disease activity, and Fab fragments are more pathogenic than intact IgG4, suggesting IgG4 Fc modulates pathogenicity. The current study provides direct evidence for IgG subclass effects and suggests a protective role for non-pathogenic IgG1 antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 accurately summarize prior literature on PF, while C123-C124 correctly position the current study's contributions. The prior work suggested but did not directly demonstrate IgG subclass effects, which the current study addresses through controlled experiments with matched antibodies.

results.result: Different antibody types have distinct requirements for optimal activity: effector antibodies require activating FcγRs, agonistic antibodies depend on inhibitory FcγRIIB, and blocking anti-PD1 antibodies function best without FcγR binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 summarize established principles about how different antibody types are affected by Fc-FcγR interactions, supported by citations to reviews and primary literature. This provides the conceptual framework for understanding why autoantibodies with different modes of action might be differentially affected by IgG subclass.

results.result: Anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies have multiple functional mechanisms: they function as blocking antibodies (inhibiting enzyme activity in the absence of FcγRs) and as effector antibodies (FcγR-mediated depletion enhances pathogenicity). Among natural IgG subclasses, IgG4 has the least effector function, making IgG4 switching protective in TTP.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C136 synthesize the TTP findings into a coherent mechanistic model. The blocking function (C130-C131) is supported by activity in FcγR-null mice and epitope requirements. The effector function (C132-C133) is inferred from FcγR-dependent enhancement of pathogenicity. The conclusion about IgG4 being protective (C136) follows logically from the data and established IgG4 properties.

results.result: Anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies primarily function as blocking antibodies (pathogenic in scFv form, require specific epitopes), but Fc-FcγR interaction attenuates pathogenicity. The protective effect is likely due to FcγR-mediated effector function promoting clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic keratinocytes, rather than agonistic function. This represents a beneficial role for FcγR-mediated clearance in tissue repair.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C145 synthesize the PF findings into a mechanistic model. The blocking function (C137-C139) is supported by prior literature and the current data. The protective role of FcγR engagement (C140-C141) is well-supported by experimental data. The mechanism (C145) is inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing enhanced clearance with GASDALIE variants. Claim C146 appropriately suggests future directions.

results.result: In anti-PD1 antibodies, FcγR-dependent depletion of PD1-expressing T cells or agonistic function reduces T cell immunity, countering the effect of blocking PD1 signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C150 accurately summarizes prior work on anti-PD1 antibodies (Dahan et al., 2015) to provide a comparative example of how Fc-FcγR interactions can counter blocking antibody function in a different context. This helps explain why blocking antibodies can be differentially affected by FcγR engagement.
